posts.title: Equal area does not establish equal friction
posts.caption:
Two rectangular ducts can have the same area without establishing the same friction loss.

Illustrative clear internal dimensions: 12 x 12 in and 6 x 24 in both give 144 in^2 = 1 ft^2. At the same volume flow and reference basis, both have the same cross-sectional mean velocity. Their perimeters differ: 48 in versus 60 in.

That geometry difference matters to a friction comparison; it is not a pressure-loss ratio. Length, roughness and fittings still matter.

Swipe through the six-slide check, then compare geometry-aware options:
https://www.anyhvac.net/tools/duct-calculator

Examples only; not recommended duct sizes.

posts.title: Two air streams. One checked air state.
posts.caption:
Mixed air needs more than an average of two temperatures.

Outdoor and return air can differ in temperature and moisture. The free AnyHVAC Mixed Air Calculator combines the streams using psychrometric mass and energy conservation.

Check both air states, their flow inputs and the common pressure. Humidity ratio and enthalpy are weighted by dry-air mass; a volume fraction is not automatically the same mass fraction.

Explore the tool:
https://www.anyhvac.net/tools/mixed-air-calculator

Ideal mixing assumptions apply. This is not a ventilation-compliance check. For future practical HVAC updates, the website newsletter is optional.

posts.title: Lower RH does not necessarily mean less moisture
posts.caption:
Lower RH does not prove moisture removal.

Warm the same air at fixed pressure without adding or removing moisture: humidity ratio stays constant, while RH falls.

Swipe for the six-slide explanation. Compare the full air state, not one reading. Concept only; not diagnosis.

posts.title: Lower RH does not necessarily mean less moisture
posts.caption:
A lower relative-humidity reading does not necessarily mean moisture was removed.

In a heating-only example at fixed pressure, with no moisture added or removed, humidity ratio stays constant while relative humidity falls as temperature rises.

RH describes vapor pressure relative to saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature. Humidity ratio describes water-vapor mass per mass of dry air. Different quantities, different questions.

Swipe through the six-slide explanation, then check the full air state:
https://www.anyhvac.net/tools/psychrometric-calculator

Concept only; not equipment diagnosis. Set matching inputs and project pressure before comparison.

posts.title: Same airflow. Different mean velocity.
posts.caption:
Same airflow. Different cross-sectional area. Different mean velocity.

For an illustrative 1,000 actual CFM on the same reference basis:
- 2 ft^2 gives 500 FPM mean velocity.
- 1 ft^2 gives 1,000 FPM mean velocity.

The relation is Q = V x A. These are arithmetic examples, not recommended velocities. A real duct change can change system airflow; this comparison does not predict fan performance.

Watch the 28-second check, then use the free Air Distribution Tools:
https://www.anyhvac.net/tools/air-distribution
